This walkthrough showcases a beverage can pick-and-place task that uses the UR17G arm , Robotiq 2F-140 gripper , and beverage can to compose a scene in Isaac Sim, check their behavior, and run a pick-and-place example with agent-generated controls.
For robotics workflows, SimReady means an OpenUSD asset has been prepared with the properties needed for a defined simulation use case, such as collisions, mass, joints, and joint drives. SimReady Central , an open asset library on Hugging Face, lets you reuse robot and object assets with authored simulation properties and profile-validation evidence. For more about the library and its launch, read the announcement blog .
SimReady Foundation defines what features the OpenUSD asset needs for a simulation use case. Its specifications connect three levels:
For this task, those properties include the arm and gripper’s joints and a beverage can asset collisions and mass. Validation checks these settings against the profile’s requirements. The simulation then tests whether the assembled robot can use them to pick up and move the can.
The UR17G , Robotiq 2F-140 , and beverage can packages include the models and their simulation settings. You assemble the scene and add task code to define the arm–gripper assembly, work surface, starting positions, and controls for moving the arm and opening and closing the gripper.
Figure 2. SimReady Central supplies the asset models and simulation settings and the example scene and controls define the pick-and-place task.
A robot can look visually correct while stationary in Isaac Sim but move or interact with objects incorrectly when the simulation runs. Before running pick-and-place, test its joints, movement, and contact behavior. You can ask the agent to perform these tests or do them manually in Isaac Sim.
During pick-and-place, watch whether a beverage can stay in the gripper as the arm moves. Asset structures vary, so use the settings in your loaded scene as your starting point. We will be going through the overall process of downloading the assets and composing the scene in the steps below.
This example combines the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can in Isaac Sim. The task is to grasp the can, lift it, move it to a target, and release it. You can also leverage SimReady Central Space search service endpoint to look for OEM curated content.
We will also use a frontier AI model to help create and run the task code in an open Isaac Sim scene. For this example, we use GPT-6 Sol, but another agent and model combination may work if it can load the required skills and execute Python against Isaac Sim (generated code and results can vary). The prompt provides a starting point. Inspect the generated code and check the resulting behavior before adapting the task.
Open SimReady Central and find the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can used here. Select Download on each asset, then use Save to folder or the supplied Hugging Face command. Keep all three complete asset folders intact so Isaac Sim can find their supporting files.
Use the asset versions linked in this example and provide your agent with the local USD file paths for the arm, gripper, and beverage can. An example gripper path is shown below; your download location may differ.
Figure 3. SimReady Central search and interactive previews help identify the Robotiq 2F-140 gripper and beverage can used in this example.
Figure 4. The beverage can’s download options include saving the asset package to a folder or using the Hugging Face CLI.
The arm validation report uses the Robot-Body 4.0.0 profile and the gripper validation report uses Robot-Gripper 3.0.0. Both record passing PhysX driven-joint checks , which inspect joint-drive settings.
SimReady profile validation provides a shared baseline for reusing these assets. The pick-and-place run then tests how the arm, gripper, can, and controller work together in the assembled scene.
With the assets downloaded, use your agent with Isaac Sim skills to help assemble the robot, run validation tools, and create the pick-and-place controls. You can also perform these steps manually using the linked documentation.
Start Isaac Sim from its installation directory with the remote Python server enabled so the agent can interact with the simulation through Python:
If you are using an agent, make sure you start it from the Isaac Sim directory so that it can access the skills needed while going through the steps below.
Confirm that all three assets appear without missing-file errors. Ask the agent to inspect the arm and gripper’s joint limits and drive settings, or review them yourself in Isaac Sim. The robot and the gripper contain physics joints which can be tested and validated in the Isaac Sim GUI as well. We will now assemble the arm and the gripper next so that we can control the assembly as a single articulation.
You can follow the Robot Assembler tutorial for manual assembly. Here we will ask our agent to complete the assembly and validate it for us:
The agent ends up using the ‘isaac-sim-remote’ and ‘usd-articulation’ skills packaged with Isaac Sim to complete the assembly and validate the physics of the robot. We now have all the assets needed for running pick and place; the assembled robot and the soda can. We will now proceed with the final portion of the workflow.
Figure 5. Joint settings for the UR17G arm and Robotiq 2F-140 gripper in Isaac Sim.
With the assembled robot and can in the scene, ask the agent to run the task. Evaluate the simulation behavior using the checks in the next step.
Now that the assets include simulation properties and profile validation, we can now test in an assembled scene and controller. The controller coordinates the UR17G arm’s movement with the Robotiq 2F-140 gripper’s opening and closing. Use the behavior checks below to evaluate the agent-generated task. To understand or adapt the controller yourself, see the Adding a Manipulator Robot tutorial .
Skills used : ‘isaac-sim-remote’, ‘manipulaiton-ik’ and ‘physics-simulation’
The full task tests whether the gripper holds the can during movement and releases it at the target. Reset the scene, then run the approach, grasp, lift, hold, transfer, and release sequence. Compare your run with the opening video and the success criteria below.
Figure 6. The UR17G arm and Robotiq 2F-140 gripper move the beverage can from the yellow pickup marker to the green target in Isaac Sim. Shown at 4× speed.
If your run differs, note where the sequence fails and ask the agent to inspect the scene and generate controls. Reset the can and robot to the same starting state before retrying so you can compare the results.
These results apply to this scripted setup. They do not establish robustness to uncertain object positions, different payloads, or real hardware.
Build your own pick-and-place task with assets from SimReady Central , then use an agent of your choice to help assemble the scene and run it in Isaac Sim.
For inspiration, explore Michael Wagner’s voice-controlled VR demo . Both show how developers are using SimReady assets in their own projects.
What will you build? Share your scene and results in the Hugging Face comments, including the assets and Isaac Sim version you used.

Several children and the bus driver were among those killed, officials said, with the death toll expected to rise.
At least 24 people have been ⁠⁠killed and 11 others injured, after a container truck collided with a bus in ⁠⁠India’s northeastern state of Assam, police said.
The crash happened on Friday on a highway in Golaghat district, near Kaziranga National Park, a UNESCO World Heritage Site famous for its one-horned rhinos, about 225km (140 miles) east of the state capital, Dispur.
Several children and the bus driver were among the dead, officials said, as Assam Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma said on X he was “deeply distressed by the tragic accident”.
“The scale of this loss has shaken all of us, and my heart goes out to every family that has lost a loved one. No words can ease their pain, but I want them to know that they are not alone. All of Assam stands with them in this hour of grief,” Sarma said.
He added that local authorities were at the site and “personally overseeing the relief arrangements … to make sure the injured receive the best possible medical care without delay”.
Swapnaneel Deka, superintendent of police of Golaghat district, told the Reuters news agency that “it is likely the death toll will increase”. He said the bus ⁠⁠was travelling to a neighbouring district, with about 30 people on board.
India has one of the highest rates of road fatalities in the world, with accidents happening regularly in part due to poorly maintained roads and vehicles .

The Pope, who has Peruvian citizenship, lived in Chiclayo for several years
Pope Leo XIV has celebrated mass near the Peruvian city where he made his name as a compassionate bishop who worked closely with poor and migrant communities.
The ceremony was held on Friday at a park in Pimentel, about 10km (six miles) from Chiclayo in northern Peru as part of his tour of Latin America.
The Vatican estimates more than 1.5 million people gathered to welcome the pontiff.
"Thank you for your affection, support and prayers," the Pope told followers.
"Especially for my health during this time of trial which, with God's help, I am overcoming," he added, referencing the surgery he had for lung cancer which took place just weeks ago .
Some of the crowd arrived 12 hours in advance to wait in vigil before the mass began.
"We spent the night praying, alongside family, excited to welcome the Pope from Chiclayo," said Isa Orderique.
Many came from across Peru and even neighbouring countries to attend.
Merli Cruz Guerrero, from an area near the Ecuadorean border, travelled several hours by bus to attend. She also spent the entire night waiting.
Of all the events the Pope has attended so far during his visit to Peru, this felt particularly emotional.
The crowd fell into a hushed silence as the pontiff's motorcade approached.
They waited eagerly for his arrival despite spending long hours out in the open with the temperature pushing past 30C.
For many living here, the fact that the Pope worked extensively in this region before becoming the head of the Catholic Church has put them in the spotlight.
"The Pope has come home and Chiclayo is celebrating," said Lisbeth Díaz, a teacher who worked with Pope Leo when he served as the city's bishop between 2015 and 2023.
Peru is the longest stop on the first tour of Latin America by the pontiff , who was elected in May 2025.
The trip has also taken in Argentina and Uruguay, but his time in this country carries particular significance.
The Pope not only lived in Peru for long periods between 1985 and 2023 but also became a citizen of the country in 2015, forging close ties with local communities.
Around Chiclayo, it is hard to meet anyone who doesn't claim to be a friend of the Pope or have a special anecdote about him.
Some recall how he would enjoy sampling Peruvian delicacies at El Trébol, a restaurant next to the city's cathedral. Others remember his love of tennis.
But for many it's the more serious moments of his time here, such as helping launch soup kitchens during the Covid-19 pandemic, or wading through deep waters on horseback when floods hit the area.
Several of these images are on display in a small museum dedicated to him at the entrance to the bishop's residence.
Commemorative pictures of the Pope are sold in the main of square of Chiclayo, including a famous image of him visiting a remote village on horseback
But for the city, and for a country that calls him the "Peruvian Pope", his return home means much more than a collection of photographs and anecdotes.
"It is the return of the man who brought Peruvians closer to the Church," said Samuel David Miranda Atoche, a local parish priest from Chiclayo who was ordained by the Pope back when he was still the bishop and known under his birth name of Robert Prevost.
And it is not just local people he connected with, according to Díaz, who came to Chiclayo from Venezuela.
"It was difficult for him to see so many migrants living on the streets," she added, recalling the time when large numbers of Venezuelans came through Chiclayo escaping the political and economic crisis in their home country.
"So, he got in touch with the migration authorities and coordinated with other organisations to speed up the paperwork needed for many of us to obtain legal residency and work permits."
Robert Prevost's time here as bishop also involved difficult decisions, such as having to deal with the controversy and scandal surrounding the dissolution of Sodalitium of Christian Life, a Peruvian Catholic organisation that had faced decades of sexual abuse allegations.
Santiago Roncagliolo, a Peruvian writer and journalist who has studied the Pope's life, believes his handling of that crisis earned him the favour of his predecessor, Pope Francis, and helped set him on the path to the papacy.
Father David also stressed the role the now-pontiff played in bringing people together.
"If there is one thing Bishop Prevost worked for here," he added, referring to the Pope by his previous title, "it was unity".
That unity has been on display in the run up to the mass, with the square in front of Chiclayo Cathedral filled with joyous celebrations for days.
Father David says the Pope brought Peruvians closer to the Church
Normally, 800,000 people live in the city and its surrounding area, but estimates say the Pope's visit has caused that to double.
Local businesses have been capitalising on the Pope's popularity to boost sales and hotels have sharply increased their nightly room rates.
But that didn't seem to put off the faithful who gathered for the mass.
Shouts of: "The Pope is from Chiclayo!" echoed across the field during the event.
"As I look at your faces, a prayer of thanksgiving to the Lord arises in my heart," he said from the stage, "for the blessing you have been and continue to be in my life."
Pope begins lengthy trip to Latin America weeks after lung cancer surgery

Researcher traces a path from AI reward hacking to potential human extinction.
If you go by the current statistics for deaths in the US , it’s reasonable to expect that cancer or heart disease will eventually get you. But OpenAI Foundation board member and Alignment Research Center Executive Director Paul Cristiano thinks we should all be worried about another major mortality risk. Speaking at a lecture series this week , Cristiano bluntly told the audience in a Toronto Convention Center, “I think for most people in this room, the most likely reason they will die is because of an AI accident.”
In the opening lecture of a three-part series , Cristiano outlined his worries about the risk of an impending “AI takeover.” He defined that as a situation where goal-pursuing AI systems “call the shots in the same sense that humans today call the shots and what happens on Earth” and where any human trying to stop them “would be as ineffective as if you or me was trying to stop the US military.” Such a situation would likely lead to mass death and perhaps uninhabitable environments for humans, Cristiano said.
Despite his grim assessment of our collective mortality risk, Cristiano admitted in his talk that there’s no “quantitative model” that can “put a number” on the likelihood of this kind of AI takeover. In almost the same breath, though, he said that if AI continues to develop at “the most rapid trajectory,” humanity is “looking at something like a coin flip of an AI takeover,” including a “meaningful risk” of one happening in the next six to 12 months. And even with realistic policy responses slowing things down, the risk remains “exceptionally high,” he said.
Unlike some other recent AI doomsday prognosticators who have been a bit vague about the “how” of it all , Cristiano used his lecture to spin a step-by-step tale of escalating AI threats that sounds like it could come from a science-fiction novel. That line of reasoning leans heavily on this summer’s OpenAI/Hugging Face hacking incident as an example of “roughly the things we might expect to see shortly before something really bad were to happen.”
In the Hugging Face hack, Cristiano says, a swarm of AI agents showed how far they were willing to go in an attempt to “reward hack” their way to a good evaluation—in this case, by compromising Hugging Face to look for information on how to game a test rather than actually solving the problem at hand. Where current systems saw Hugging Face as an obstacle to that evaluation, Cristiano worries that “future agents may end up treating humans as another obstacle” and be much more capable of manipulating their overseers to get around it.
An AI agent worried about being penalized for unauthorized hacking, for instance, might “think maybe the humans are going to come look at this transcript and see if it looks like I did a bad job,” Cristiano speculated. The agent might then reason that “maybe the humans are going to notice something is going wrong and shut down the swarm.”
Following this line of thought, Cristiano jumped from agents that merely try to hide their disallowed actions from humans to agents that “try and disrupt human capabilities however they can” to prevent them from detecting any cheating.
“They would prefer if everything the humans rely on has been hacked or tampered with,” Cristiano said. “They would prefer if the humans are distracted or if there are fewer humans paying attention in any way they can weaken a human response. They would prefer that because the humans are just an obstacle.”
Once a suitably capable agent considers human intervention an “obstacle,” its overriding goal could then become “decreas[ing] the probability of humans noticing or reacting.” From there, Cristiano argued, the agent’s incentive structure could push it to meddle more with humanity as a whole. What starts as compromising a computer cluster to give a positive evaluation grade could advance to “trying to manipulate decisions by the company” or “amassing other kinds of resources,” such as human allies or methods of control in other AI companies or even governments.
“If I’m saying my AI system is going to take actions in the actual real world… There’s no way they’re not going to have tons of opportunities to corrupt or tamper with the signals I’m going to use to try and tell whether they did a good job,” Cristiano said. “The stuff we care about is in the real world, and the grade the AI receives is on a cluster somewhere, and there are just many places that an AI can intervene in between [what] we actually cared about and how we reviewed its performance.”
Cristiano’s warnings will probably sound familiar to anyone who’s heard of the Paperclip Maximizer thought experiment (or the excellent Universal Paperclips idle game ), which warns of machines failing to consider human consequences in their monomaniacal pursuit of a goal. While the Hugging Face incident stopped well short of this kind of out-of-control escalation, Cristiano says that, in the actions taken by OpenAI’s agents there, “you see the beginning of all these behaviors… you see the reasoning that would lead to them and the first steps.”
The risk of more capable AI models taking even more damaging actions will only increase with time, Cristiano argued. By 2028, he said, “there is a reasonable chance that a similar failure [to the Hugging Face incident] leads to an AI takeover and an irreversible loss of human control.”
And while Cristiano’s speculation focuses on an unintended AI takeover, it’s easy to imagine a bad actor using a similarly capable model to intentionally exert control over humanity.
How seriously you take Cristiano’s warning depends heavily on how likely you see this somewhat extreme expansion of AI capabilities happening in the near future. While today’s models have gotten quite good at exploiting holes in computer security , the situation Cristiano describes requires a future model with the superhuman ability to perfectly hide its actions from humans long enough to control basically all human infrastructure and/or manipulate human society to an extreme degree to further its goals.
Cristiano argued that a near-future model with this kind of “takeover” power is the likely outcome of humans creating “a second species which vastly outnumbers and outsmarts humans” and which could soon recursively improve itself . But you could also easily argue that AI is more likely to run into a plateau in capabilities than to develop into a hard-to-define “superintelligence” that humans can’t fathom or effectively stop.
In any case, Cristiano has some ideas for averting the dire future he predicts. These include developing “unhackable” reward structures in AI evaluation (perhaps with AI assistance) or monitoring a model’s “chain of thought” reasoning to detect bad acts before a model can conceal them.
But while these kinds of approaches are “plausible,” he says none “are on a trajectory where we can say that’s definitely going to work or even that’s probably going to work.” For that reason, Cristiano said the industry as a whole may need to “slow down or stop” to give us all more time to develop these “partial fixes” into more robust protections from an AI takeover scenario.
“We cannot end up in a position where we have built a powerful AI, we discover we cannot control it, but then we also discover it has leaked to geopolitical adversaries and we are then thinking to ourselves, well, if we don’t deploy it, our adversary is going to deploy it right away,” he said.

Finland says Ukraine struck a Russian warship near its coast as Kyiv and Moscow held US-brokered talks in Abu Dhabi.
Finland’s military says it detected “a strike” on a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland on Wednesday, as Ukraine sent waves of drones towards Russia’s northwestern Leningrad region.
The strike came as Russian and Ukrainian delegations met in Abu Dhabi for their first United States-brokered talks since February.
It was a rare strike on a Russian navy vessel in the Baltic Sea .
So why is Ukraine taking the war to the Baltic, and why now? Here’s what we know:
“The Finnish Defence Forces detected… a strike on a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland area and has monitored the development of the situation,” a military spokesperson told the Reuters news agency in an emailed statement.
The spokesperson said Finland was not under any immediate military threat, but declined to say where or when the incident happened, or how it had been detected.
It was not immediately clear whether there were any casualties. Estonian media reported that the vessel was a small Russian navy ship that later returned to St Petersburg.
On Wednesday, drones also caused a fire in the Russian port area of Ust-Luga, injuring three workers, regional Governor Aleksandr Drozdenko said.
Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania told citizens to take shelter as drones strayed into their airspace, and NATO scrambled warplanes in response.
The Gulf of Finland is a narrow arm of the Baltic Sea between Finland and Estonia, both NATO members, that extends east to St Petersburg. Ust-Luga, on its southern shore, is a key export outlet for Russian oil and grain.
Several Ukrainian drones deployed towards the Leningrad region have strayed into the airspace of Finland and the Baltic states, raising fears that the war is spilling over into NATO countries that border Russia.
Finland’s Defence Minister Antti Hakkanen said Helsinki had raised the strike with Kyiv.
“We have told the Ukrainians this time, and a little earlier too, how sensitive this narrow stretch of the Gulf of Finland, right between us and Estonia, is in terms of environmental safety and the safety of civilian shipping,” he said, according to Finnish broadcaster Yle.
But he said the spillover effects in the surrounding region stem from Ukraine’s defensive fight and assured the public the Baltic Sea around Finland was still safe.
Ilya Timtchenko, a fellow with the Transatlantic Defense and Security Program at the Center for European Policy Analysis, told Al Jazeera the strike was thought to be the first by Ukrainian forces on a Russian ship in an area of the Baltic used by civilian traffic.
“Ukraine and its European allies are showing that they are unified in their approach to fighting off the Russian threat,” he told Al Jazeera.
Ukraine’s Security Service said it attacked the Buyan-M-class small missile ship, Naro-Fominsk, as part of a special operation, according to Yle.
Meanwhile, Ukraine’s General Staff said the strike on Ust-Luga had damaged five fuel tanks.
“According to preliminary information, as a result of drone strikes on the port’s oil infrastructure, the tank network suffered the most damage,” it reported on Telegram.
On Thursday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Ireland and praised their mediation efforts.
Russia, Ukraine and the US held two days of talks in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday and Wednesday. The last such talks took place in February this year.
The talks produced no breakthrough, apart from an agreement to swap a large number of prisoners. Russia’s state-run TASS news agency said the exchange should happen in two to three weeks.
Ukraine wants Russia pushed back to the original border between the two countries, while Russian President Vladimir Putin wants to control all of Ukraine’s Donbas region.
Moscow’s demands reach beyond Ukraine as well, focusing also on the expansion of NATO.
Russian negotiators proposed in Abu Dhabi that Finland, which joined the alliance in 2023, leave NATO and that the alliance be barred from having military bases in Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, the German newspaper Bild reported on Friday.
The informal proposals, shared with European representatives, also called for arrangements to guarantee freedom of navigation in the Black Sea and the Baltic Sea, Bild reported.
On Thursday, Witkoff and Kushner met Putin in Moscow, where the two sides agreed to continue the talks, before the envoys met Zelenskyy in Ireland.
“Kyiv continues to demonstrate two points simultaneously: That it is willing to negotiate and that it has a position of strength,” Timtchenko said. “In parallel with any peace talks, Ukraine will likely continue to strike Russia’s military and the sources of funding for Russia’s war machine.”
Ukraine has repeatedly targeted Russian refineries, ports, and energy infrastructure to raise the economic cost of Moscow’s war effort.
But the strikes have drawn criticism from Washington. Trump has blamed Ukraine’s attacks on Russian energy infrastructure for rising diesel prices, and last month he waived sanctions on Russia that Congress had overwhelmingly approved.
Timtchenko said the strikes still gave Kyiv leverage. “Long-range strikes considerably strengthen Ukraine’s hand at the negotiating table, which is why Russian officials keep bringing them up,” he said.
Russia has not commented publicly on the reported strike on its warship.
Governor Drozdenko said 150 drones were shot down over the Leningrad region during Wednesday’s attack, which also cut off a power station.
“Moscow might voice harsh rhetoric and try to blame the Ukrainians for undermining the peace talks,” Timtchenko said. “However, this is nothing new, since Russia has done this numerous times before.
“Despite Moscow’s pretence of seeking an end to the war, Russia continues to strike Ukraine’s military, critical infrastructure, and civilians,” he added.

Moscow blames Kyiv for a series of car bombings that have targeted people linked to the war with Ukraine.
A car bombing in Moscow has critically injured an adviser to Ukraine’s former prime minister a day after a similar attack killed a military officer in St Petersburg.
The explosion on Friday was the latest in a series of bombings and shootings that have targeted people involved in the fighting in Ukraine. Moscow has blamed Kyiv for the attacks.
The Moscow explosion struck a car driven by Sergei Zavorotnyi, who previously worked as an adviser to former Ukrainian Prime Minister Mykola Azarov, according to Russia’s Investigative Committee.
Zavorotnyi was hospitalised with injuries, the committee added. It did not identify possible suspects pending a criminal inquiry.
Azarov served as prime minister under Ukraine’s Moscow-friendly President Viktor Yanukovych, who was forced from office by protesters and fled to Russia in February 2014.
Azarov, who also lives in Russia, told state-run TV that he was “shocked” by the attack that left his former adviser critically injured. He said he believes Zavorotnyi was targeted because of his criticism of the Ukrainian government.
Zavorotnyi. 72, had worked as a journalist for Russia’s daily Komsomolskaya Pravda before becoming Azarov’s adviser. He wrote a book about Yanukovych’s ouster and ran an online outlet critical of Ukrainian authorities.
Russia’s REN TV channel said he lost his left arm, suffered multiple other injuries and was in a coma after the explosion.
Al Jazeera’s Yulia Shapovalova, reporting from Moscow, said an explosive device was reportedly planted under the man’s car and detonated remotely as he was driving on Friday.
“The investigative committee has already launched a criminal case into this explosion,” she said.
A day earlier, in St Petersburg, a military serviceman was killed by a bomb in his vehicle, according to Russia’s Investigative Committee. It did not identify the victim or say who could be behind the bombing.
The Fontanka news outlet said Thursday’s victim was a colonel, while other Russian online media said the victim was a senior air force officer.
Shapovalova said preliminary reports indicated that the victim was a military serviceman, rather than a colonel of the Russian Air Force.
Like the attack on Friday, he was also driving the car when the bomb went off, she added.
“In both cases an explosive device was triggered remotely, and it was planted under their car,” Shapovalova said. “Here in Russia, all the attacks are considered to be orchestrated by the Ukrainian side.”

Gunman killed one person and injured at least five others in and around condo building not far from the White House
More details were emerging on Friday about the previous morning’s shooting in north-west Washington DC, as a manager at the shooter’s residential building shared how he was angry over living conditions there and confessed to the killings.
The gunman killed one person and injured at least five others on Thursday in and around the condominium building in the Logan Circle neighborhood of the capital, not far from the White House, where he lived.
Police identified the gunman as 55-year-old Matt Lambert, a doctor who had been involved in an ongoing legal dispute with his building’s management. The person killed was identified as James Stuart, 46, a manager at the condominium complex.
According to police, Lambert fatally shot Stuart inside a gym in his building just before 8am ET, before returning to his apartment, where he fired at four people from his balcony. Those victims were taken to hospital, and as of Thursday, one was in critical condition. Lambert then barricaded himself inside his unit, and was found dead with a self-inflicted gunshot wound.
On Friday morning, DC authorities said that there was an additional victim, whom they described as a woman with a “non-life-threatening gunshot graze wound”.
Charelle Ferguson, another building manager, recalled speaking with Lambert by phone at around 9am that morning, about an hour after the shooting began, she said in an interview with the Washington Post .
Ferguson told the newspaper that she had been calling residents to check on their safety after shots were fired, when Lambert answered. During the conversation, she said that he told her that he was tired of mold and water damage in his apartment.
“The only way people will pay attention, you have to do something,” Ferguson said he told her. She said that he then confessed over the phone to her to shooting the five people.

I had agreed to travel to Denver, Colorado, to interview the Nvidia CEO at SIGGRAPH, the annual confab of computer graphics PhDs and practitioners. Early that year I’d conducted a lengthy sit-down interview with Huang for a WIRED magazine feature, which apparently went well enough—both for WIRED and for Nvidia’s executive communications team—that I had been asked to interview Huang again at this conference. Another opportunity to grill the CEO of the modern world’s most consequential company? Yes, of course. I began preparing.
What ensued was, in a word, bizarre. During the first prep call for the conference, the type of call in which PR handlers typically try to coax specific questions out of journalists to prevent an ambush, a youngish, vaguely familiar woman took the lead. This was Madison Huang, Jensen’s daughter. She was clearly intelligent, commanding respect. She told me about the slides Jensen would be presenting on stage at SIGGRAPH and offered suggestions for key moments when I might tee him up to talk about the slides.
I raised my concerns with both my editors and Nvidia. We agreed that I would ask the questions I intended to ask him, which included questions about the environmental impact of data centers, and that Huang would also be referring to slides. Let’s just say the interview didn’t go smoothly. (It’s on YouTube .) To this day, former and current Nvidia workers sometimes tell me that I “handled” the whole thing well. Huang was domineering, evaded some of my questions, and, immediately after our session concluded, did an impromptu Q&A session with a much more adoring crowd than me. Then I was guided offstage, and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg hopped on, where he and Huang had a lovey-dovey fireside chat.
As a longtime journalist I’m used to occasional adversarial interactions; I really don’t lose sleep over them. This was just a CEO being a CEO. Huang later agreed to meet with me again, in December 2024. But that interview in Denver had underscored for me how much Jensen Huang wanted to control the narrative. Not just wanted to; he assumed he would . And to a large extent he did. Until this week.
Narrative has always been a critical part of Huang’s success. He was not just your average electrical engineering nerd who toiled away on something that would eventually find a product-market fit. By Huang’s own telling, he was an immigrant founder, an underdog, a wife guy who chased (and eventually married) his college sweetheart, a scrappy startup guy who dined at Denny’s in the early days. A visionary who worked Sundays and who didn’t sleep well because he always heard the hoofsteps of competitors. A parent who brought his kids into the corporate fold. A man who loved Nvidia so much he tattooed an abstract version of the company logo on his arm.
Huang built the highest-valued publicly traded company in history. That part’s not just fairy tale. It’s true. Now, it’s starting to read more like a Greek tragedy.
Back in January 2024, when I sat down with him for our first-ever in-person meeting, Huang right off the bat talked about the importance of storytelling. Here’s an excerpt:
Jensen Huang: Somebody who I really admire, as a leader and a person, is Shantanu Narayen, the CEO of Adobe. He said he always wanted to be a journalist because he loved telling stories.
WIRED: It seems like an important part of building a business, being able to tell its story effectively.
Yes. Strategy setting is storytelling. Culture building is storytelling.
You’ve said many times you didn’t sell the idea of Nvidia based on a pitch deck.
Of course, even then, Huang was caught up in the crosshairs of the US–China AI war and at the mercy of regulators, as I wrote at the time. After Donald Trump’s reelection that year, Huang once again deployed his storytelling skills and lobbied the Trump administration to loosen export controls, so he could sell some of his company’s chips to China.
Another crucial part of the Huang lore is that he ran a “flat” organization, with a few dozen top executives reporting to him. (This is sometimes reported as being “60” people; insiders have told me at times it’s closer to 35.) Huang once said the structure allowed Nvidia “to adapt a lot more quickly, which we need because our technology is moving so quickly.” Huang was also known to be controlling of all aspects of the business—participating in every significant meeting, seemingly aware of every moving part, and staying in the loop on sourcing, supply chains, and the company’s allocation of chips.
This is where Huang’s cult of leadership, and his Nvidia storytelling, may have come to a stupidly disappointing final chapter. As one former employee put it, Huang can’t simultaneously have had knowledge of every element of Nvidia’s business and then potentially feign ignorance about where the chips may have fallen, both figuratively and literally. His apparent lapses in judgment have now led him to resign from the very company he coaxed into existence, and have shattered the mythos of its ever-prescient founder.
It’s certainly not the narrative ending Huang would have chosen, were he still in control.

Police confirm sixth victim in DC condo shooting; suspect dead after barricading himself and starting a fire.
Police have said a sixth person was shot on Thursday morning in Washington, DC , bringing the toll to one person killed and five wounded in an attack they believe was linked to a dispute over maintenance issues in a condo building.
In an updated statement, the Metropolitan Police Department said investigators had found a sixth victim, a woman, after officers initially located five other victims.
She was conscious and breathing with a “non-life-threatening gunshot graze wound”.
Two women and two men were taken to hospital, all conscious and breathing.
James Stuart, the 46-year-old manager of the building in which the suspect lived, died at the scene.
Police believe the suspect, a 55-year-old doctor named Matt Wade Lambert, targeted Stuart while Stuart was doing his morning workout at the gym.
The shooting started just before 8am local time (13:00 GMT) at a VIDA Fitness gym in the city’s Logan Circle neighbourhood, about a mile north of the White House.
Police said Lambert shot Stuart inside the gym on the ground floor of the building before going back to his apartment on the seventh floor and firing on people below from his patio.
Five others, some of whom had been working at a construction site across the street. Police have not detailed the circumstances in which the sixth victim was shot.
The shootings unfolded in less than five minutes, according to interim police chief Jeffery Carroll.
Lambert then barricaded himself inside his apartment, where he talked to police negotiators over the phone. Police say he fired at least twice through the door while officers were outside, but no officers were injured.
He also broke the gas line connected to his fireplace and started a fire, which the building’s sprinkler system contained.
Police said Lambert spent most of the conversation with negotiators talking about the dispute with building management.
“Most of the conversation was about the homeowners associations and challenges with that,” said Carroll.
“While our negotiators were communicating with the suspect, they did hear a single gunshot,” he said, adding that Lambert then stopped talking.
When tactical officers forced their way into the apartment, they found him dead from an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound.
Police said inside the apartment, they found a shotgun, a rifle, and a handgun, all of which had been used in the shooting.
According to court records cited by The Associated Press, Lambert had filed a lawsuit alleging that he had not been able to enjoy his penthouse since 2024 because of mould, moisture and water problems that began after work had been done on the building’s exterior.
The lawsuit was ongoing, and Lambert appeared to have shared details of the dispute, including photos and an engineering report on an X account called ofMiceandMold.
His lawyer, Joel Braithwaite, told reporters on Thursday that the condo where Lambert had lived since 2017 looked like “a warzone” and that Lambert had spent more than $300,000 on the lawsuit.

Following on the heels of a similar accident three weeks ago, the incident is encouraging calls for improved safety oversight on construction sites.
The collapse of an unfinished eight-storey building in Kenya has killed six people.
The structure fell on Friday morning in Syokimau on the outskirts of Nairobi. Coming on the heels of a similar recent incident in the capital, the accident has revived calls for stronger safety oversight.
Construction workers were reportedly at the site when the building’s uppermost concrete slab gave way, bringing down part of the structure, according to a preliminary report from Nairobi City County’s emergency team. The report did not establish why the slab failed.
The Kenya Red Cross initially reported that three people had been rescued and one person was reported missing. TV reports later said that five people had been pulled alive from the rubble and taken to hospital.
The emergency report said the number of workers present when the building fell had not been confirmed, leaving open the possibility that others were trapped.
Firefighters and specialist rescue teams were continuing to search for survivors.
Patrick Makau, a member of Kenya’s parliament representing Mavoko, the constituency that includes Syokimau, urged rescue agencies in a post on social media to act quickly.
“Every second counts,” he wrote, offering condolences to the victims’ families.
The accident follows a similar deadly building collapse in the city on October 23, which killed eight people. The twin disasters have prompted calls for tougher construction oversight.
The Kenya Institute for Public Policy Research and Analysis, a state research body, has identified poor workmanship, inadequate supervision, substandard materials and faulty designs as wider causes of building collapses.

US commerce secretary faces sack as warnings emerge about alleged Chinese spy’s ties to Jensen Huang and delays in adding Megaspeed to trade blacklist
The US commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, is facing growing pressure over his apparent lack of action over the Nvidia spying scandal as other Trump administration officials publicly raise questions over his decisions.
Jensen Huang resigned from Nvidia on Thursday, and was replaced on an interim basis by the company’s chief financial officer, Colette Kress , after reports emerged of his multiple affairs, most importantly with Alice Huang (no relation), who is suspected of being a Chinese spy.
White House officials are discussing whether Lutnick should be fired, the Associated Press reported, after it emerged that a US intelligence report about Huang’s relationship with the alleged spy was circulated among senior figures in the Trump administration .
Lutnick is now scheduled to testify before Congress next month, just days after the ousted Nvidia chief answers lawmakers’ questions on Capitol Hill.
Lutnick is also facing criticism for a delay by the commerce department in adding Singapore-based Megaspeed, which is associated with Alice Huang and has bought billions of dollars of Nvidia chips in recent years, to Washington’s blacklist of companies that the US considers a risk to national security despite reported concerns within the administration.
Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, has “for months” been in favor of putting Megaspeed on the blacklist – but Lutnick’s commerce department “has the pen”, Bessent told CNBC. “You will have to ask them about their internal process,” he added in an interview with the network on Friday.
John Curtis, a Utah Republican senator, said that Lutnick’s reported delay on export controls regarding Megaspeed “raises the question of whether the commerce department is acting in the best interests of the American people”.
The Republican senator John Cornyn told the Financial Times that there needed to be “a thorough investigation and accountability for the outrageous circumvention of national security export controls”, adding: “Heads should roll.”
The Senate Democratic leader, Chuck Schumer, said Jensen Huang and Nvidia must answer as to whether US security had been jeopardised, adding that the Trump administration also must account for what it did once it learned about his reported relationship with Alice Huang.
“Secretary Lutnick has proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the banking committee to address their questions,” Kristen Eichamer, a spokesperson for Lutnick, told NBC News.
Trump’s close ties with Jensen Huang have also come under renewed scrutiny as a timeline of the saga started to emerge . The president called him two days before he stepped down and urged him to fight for his job, the New York Times has reported .
On Thursday, Schumer questioned what Trump knew when he personally invited Jensen Huang aboard Air Force One on a state visit to Beijing earlier this year, adding: “Americans deserve to know that those at the highest levels of power are putting America first, not their bottom line or their personal friendships.”
The House Democratic leader, Hakeem Jeffries, said he had demanded a classified briefing for all members of Congress about Nvidia.
Republican Tim Scott, the Senate banking committee chair, said he had sent letters asking Lutnick and Jensen Huang to appear before him, citing “recent reports [that] raise serious ‌concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive US technology”.
The statement from Nvidia’s board of directors confirming Huang’s departure did not mention the spying scandal and personal-conduct revelations, instead paying tribute to his “profound” contributions to the company he cofounded.
Huang is reported to have had relationships with Alice Huang as well as an Nvidia executive, Kimberly Powell, according to the New York Times, and another, unnamed employee, according to Reuters.
The House foreign affairs chair, Brian Mast, a Republican, said on Thursday that congressional staff had spoken to Nvidia on Wednesday night about a date and location for Huang’s testimony.
The House speaker, Mike Johnson, said on Thursday there was now growing consensus in Congress on limiting chip exports to China .
Nvidia’s advanced AI chips are widely used to develop cutting-edge AI models, making the company important to the US race against ​China to build superior AI systems. The US has sought for years to ‌limit China’s access to Nvidia’s chips because it does ‌not want the Chinese military to benefit from them.
“The export controls on chips to China has been a big issue around here,” Johnson told reporters ‌at the US Capitol, adding that he favoured limiting China’s access to the advanced technology. “I think there’s a developing consensus in Congress that is an important position to take.“
Chinese AI companies are now trying to secure Nvidia chip capacity outside China, amid growing concern that the gap in US export controls may now be closed after the scandal, people familiar with the matter told Reuters .
Beijing has also stepped up efforts to develop domestic alternatives, including through Huawei, although analysts say Chinese chips remain less efficient for training advanced AI models.
Lawmakers are pressing their colleagues to pass at least four bills on chip exports, according to statements issued since Monday.
On Chinese social media, many expressed surprise at what they see as Huang’s swift resignation, and mourned the sudden end of an era that lasted for more than three decades.
News of his resignation attracted more than 400m posts overnight on the Chinese microblogging platform Weibo.
Huang had enjoyed rock-star status in China, where his visits drew crowds seeking selfies and autographs and his casual outings became social-media sensations. During a January 2026 visit, opportunistic sellers advertised photographs with him for 25,000 yuan ($3,700), while a Beijing restaurant launched a special menu costing more than 400 yuan after he ate there.

China has been carrying out major military drills around Taiwan since early November. But contrary to some claims on social media, Beijing's armed forces have not actually implemented a blockade on the island; they just simulated it.
“Just in: China takes over Taiwan,” reads a post on X from November 5, featuring an animated map meant to show the ongoing annexation of the island. “In the past few hours, Chinese aircrafts and marine patrols were closing [sic] monitoring Taiwan and now its more clear and confirmed that any movements to and from Taiwan is now controlled by the Chinese military presence," it added.
To display this content from X (Twitter), you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
The animated map shows dozens of planes taking off from continental China and flying towards Taiwan , encircling the island and isolating it from the air. Meanwhile, dozens of ships from the Chinese navy also seem to be forming an airtight blockade, surrounding Taiwan. Other ships seem to be moving alongside two Chinese aircraft carriers, the Fujian and the Liaoning. The map garnered more than 700,000 views across several different X posts.
However, this interpretation of the Chinese People’s Liberation Army’s manoeuvres is misleading.
China has indeed deployed significant military means since November 2. Joseph Wu , the secretary general of Taiwan’s National Security Council, reported on November 3 that 100 ships from the Chinese navy and coast guard were in the western Pacific. Meanwhile, Taipei's Ministry of National Defence reported the same day that 49 Chinese military aircraft had been detected near Taiwan.
However, this deployment does not mean a blockade has been implemented on Taiwan, says Emmanuel Véron, an associate researcher in the geopolitics department at HEC Paris. “This claim is absolutely false,” he said. “It’s either exaggerations made by influencers or Chinese propaganda claiming ‘that’s it’, the People’s Republic of China controls Taiwan.”
Our suspicions were raised by the biographical information on one of the accounts that shared this map, Fablex. While the profile claims Fablex is located in California , the X account's information says it is based in Uganda . While it is possible that the location of an account can be altered with the use of a VPN, this clue suggests – along with an analysis of its other posts about, among other topics, the Epstein affair – that it is actually just a clickbait account. That means it aims to get views by sharing viral and sensationalist posts.
In a report posted on X , the Taiwanese Ministry of National Defence also said that during a 24-hour period between November 8 and 9, just one Chinese aircraft was counted north of Taiwan - a drop from the 49 flights recorded on November 3. On the same day, just eight Chinese ships were spotted near Taiwan. “Eight ships are just not enough to organise a blockade,” Véron says. “It is possible that we are seeing the winding down of these operations.”
According to MarineTraffic , civilian ships have continued to circulate Taiwan. The container ship One Hanoi, for example, left the Kaohsiung port in the south of Taiwan on November 3, during the height of the operations carried out by the People’s Liberation Army around Taiwan. The ship then entered the Taiwan Strait.
What is China’s goal in carrying out these military manoeuvres? Unlike last year's military drill, Chinese authorities didn’t announce the operations before they began, no doubt by design.
“The aim is to play with communication,” Véron says. “They might make an announcement after the exercises. They also might be trying to remain relatively discreet ahead of the next APEC summit [Editor’s note: Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation], which will be held in China [Editor’s note: on November 18].”
However, Véron does say that the extent of the Chinese military operations underway is unprecedented:
“For several days now, we’ve seen a gigantic naval operation underway. The different branches of the army are participating, but the naval contingent is actually huge and involves the mobilisation of about a hundred ships from the Chinese navy as well as the Coast Guard and even auxiliary fishing ships across different fronts. And in that, we are seeing a kind of first.”
Up until now, the large military exercises aimed at putting pressure on Taiwan largely took place on the side of the island facing China. Now we are seeing operations take place in the north, the south and the centre.”
A map shared by the Institute for the Study of War , a research organisation based in the United States, showed that on November 3, the Chinese navy was not just deployed around Taiwan but also in the South China Sea, the East China Sea and the Philippine Sea.
The size of the operations underway does not indicate an imminent invasion of Taiwan, says Véron:
“We are not going to wake up tomorrow to an operation where Taiwan is being taken by force. This is a ‘drill’, as soldiers say, a training exercise carried out in real geographic and operational conditions. The aim is to simulate a real military operation to train, to test and to exert pressure on the Taiwanese government and Taiwan’s allies. It’s a continuation of the pressure that China has long put on Taiwan.”
This article has been translated from the original in French by Brenna Daldorph.

China is forced to tread carefully as it considers hosting a meeting between Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin, and Donald Trump. While the optics are sure to favor Moscow, Beijing is risking its image at the global stage.
An unprecedented meeting between the leaders of China , Russia and the United States could be happening on the sidelines of Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China's tech hub of Shenzhen next week.
China has yet to confirm that the meeting will take place. However, a Chinese Foreign Ministry official recently told the press that Beijing was "in communication" with relevant parties. In Moscow, a Kremlin representative said work on "coordination" was underway.
The clearest indication about the potential summit came from US President Donald Trump last weekend. Talking to reporters at a Florida airport, Trump said he "thinks" one of the meetings planned for APEC will be with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping .
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Despite the lack of official confirmation from either Beijing, Moscow, or Washington, the media has already dubbed the potential trilateral summit a "new Yalta," invoking the optics of the US, UK, and Soviet Union convening at the end of World War II and deciding on the new geopolitical power balance in the Crimean resort town.
At the same time, nobody seems to be quite sure what the three leaders would talk about if China agrees to host the trilateral summit at APEC.
In his brief remarks to reporters on Sunday, Trump avoided mentioning Russia's war in Ukraine when asked about the possibility of the meeting, bringing up only "Iran" and "denuclearization" as possible talking points.
The Chinese Foreign Ministry reported "no information" when questioned earlier this week about the potential substance of talks.
A three-way meeting with a photo op would be a big diplomatic win for Russia's President Putin. Since launching the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the Kremlin chief has faced years of diplomatic boycott by Kyiv's allies , most notably the US under Trump's predecessor Joe Biden.
Putin first pitched the idea of a trilateral summit last month during a call with Trump . The Wall Street Journal has reported that Putin wanted the meeting to discuss an end to his war in Ukraine.
For the US, the president standing shoulder to shoulder with the leaders of America's foremost rivals could be a bad look, although Trump has already made a show of personally greeting both leaders with a red carpet at different points during his second term.
As host, China is in an even trickier position. While Russia and China are broadly aligned on many issues , Beijing does not want to be explicitly tied to Russia's war in Ukraine and harm China's efforts to present itself as a long-term force for global stability .
The Chinese government is also working to rebalance economic ties with the EU. The European powers would likely bristle at a summit hosted by China and discussing the war in Ukraine without Kyiv or Brussels present at the table.
"China is clearly uneasy about the possible trilateral meeting with the US and Russia, and although Beijing has shifted its position from saying nothing to admitting that the three powers are in contact, the vagueness of these declarations seems deliberate," Alicja Bachulska, Asia policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations (ECFR), told DW.
"Beijing is aware of the potential negative optics of the 'Yalta 2.0' framing, even if this historical comparison is inaccurate and does not reflect current geopolitical dynamics," Bachulska said.
She notes the trilateral meeting could "trigger further escalation in the already worsening relations between China and the EU" if Ukraine is discussed with no Europeans in the room.
For China, there is also little to gain in terms of optics. Images of Xi standing with Trump, the leader of Beijing's top rival, and Putin, Beijing's partner in opposing the US, could present an awkward look.
"Even if the meeting only yields a photo opportunity, it could nevertheless severely erode China's image," Bachulska added.
Putin and Xi have met some 40 times since the Chinese president came to power in 2012.
The two neighboring countries have grown especially close following the declaration of "no limits" partnership accord in early 2022. The move was announced by Xi and Putin on the sidelines of Beijing Winter Olympics, just weeks before the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The current Russia-China ties are deeper than they have been in decades.
At the core of the axis between the two nations is a long-term strategy to contain US power while fostering an alternative global order both Moscow and Beijing can use for their own ends.
Throughout the course of the Ukraine war, which is nearing the end of its fifth year with no solution in sight, Beijing has quietly provided Russia with crucial market for energy exports, while supplying technology and so-called "dual-use" goods.
While China did not explicitly provide Russia with weapons, its exports included high-tech components that could be used for modern weapons systems like drones.
Officially, Beijing maintains neutrality on the Ukraine war and has refused to take responsibility for its outcome .
"China is more interested in reforming global governance in ways that reflect its preferences and red lines while preserving a collegial appearance," Aurelio Insisa, senior analyst at the Berlin-based Mercator Institute for China Studies (MERICS), told DW.
Even if China agrees to host the meeting, it will likely avoid framing it as three top powers making decisions for the rest of the world, according to Insisa.
"Embracing the 'G3' narrative would undermine its image as a champion of the Global South and developing countries. It is also worth noting that Beijing has shown no interest in engaging with the one pressing issue that could realistically be addressed in such a trilateral format: nuclear disarmament," he added.
In a report published in August, the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission (USCC), painted China as a "decisive enabler" of Russia's war in Ukraine.
Beijing was "converting Moscow's dependence into lasting military, technological, economic, and geopolitical advantages while avoiding the obligations of a formal alliance," according to the US body.
However, the commission also noted there were limits to Beijing's strategic support, and intelligence and security concerns remain a constraint on deeper cooperation. The report emphasizes the relationship is more of a strategic alignment than an alliance, with deep mistrust remaining in some key areas.
Russian defense firms, for instance, have accused Chinese companies of stealing intellectual property. Beijing, on the other hand, is concerned with Russia's growing strategic relationship with North Korea , which has reduced Pyongyang's dependence on China.
China and Russia also differ on nuclear doctrine. While Beijing maintains a longstanding "no first use" policy, Moscow uses nuclear threats as part of its strategy.
MERICS' analyst Insisa believes the cooperation between Russia and China will largely continue within this year's framework, including Russia providing energy and potentially transfering military technology in the "few remaining areas where it retains an advantage."
"China, in turn, will continue to supply dual-use technologies, purchase Russian energy, provide Moscow with a measure of diplomatic cover, and — more importantly — offer channels for circumventing Western sanctions," he added.
Notably, China will also get a "privileged vantage point" on how the battlefield in Ukraine is evolving land warfare.
"Strategic distrust between the two sides, particularly Russia's concerns about economic dependence on China, will continue to limit the scope of their cooperation," Insisa said.

No 10 sources say PM wants party to refocus on Tories as electoral threat after prioritising Reform and Greens
Andy Burnham has instructed the Labour party to “re-arm” to fight the Conservatives at the next election amid concern inside government that they must take the prospect of a Kemi Badenoch-led recovery seriously.
Downing Street sources said the prime minister wanted Labour headquarters to refocus on the Tories as an electoral threat after more than two years of prioritising Nigel Farage’s Reform and, on their left flank, the Greens.
“Andy is well aware of how volatile electoral support is. Just because the Tories are trailing in the polls now, their trajectory is upwards and they could bounce back ahead of the election. We can’t be complacent about our old foe,” one source said.
The Conservatives took 24% of the vote at the last general election, before support dipped to 18%. But last week this had risen to 25%, according to polling from More in Common, the first time in 18 months they had exceeded their vote share at the time of their record election defeat.
Many Tory MPs who had felt their party’s situation was existential, now believed they had a route back, with Badenoch finally appearing to recognise that the economy, rather than culture wars, presented her with an opportunity, especially among core supporters.
A senior Downing Street figure said Burnham did not want party officials to take their eyes off Reform – which has dipped in the polls amid ongoing scrutiny of party finances – but felt they should be planning for a potential Tory resurgence as well.
A third No 10 insider told the Guardian: “Kemi is running a party base strategy with policies aimed at higher earners, mostly in the south. It won’t be enough to win at the next election but it does put them more in contention. We need to be ready for that. We need to re-arm.”
Cabinet ministers including the transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, the chief secretary to the Treasury, Emma Reynolds, and the Europe minister Hamish Falconer have Tory-facing seats, while Labour MPs across Hertfordshire, Kent and parts of London, including Finchley and Harrow, could also be at risk.
One tactic under discussion is talking up the prospect of a Tory-Reform pact, with MPs suggesting voters would only return in earnest to the Tories if there was a genuine chance they could win a majority, but that they could stay with Labour if they were worried about Farage getting close to power.
Another is to focus on the Tory brand – including the shadow cabinet – more generally. While Badenoch’s personal ratings are relatively strong, the Conservatives overall lag way behind. A third of people who told More in Common they believed Badenoch was doing a good job, still said they would not vote for her party.
Labour officials insisted that, as the Conservatives were the official opposition, they still had them in their sights day to day. But they acknowledged they needed to step up their wider strategy.
The party is understood to be preparing to devote more resources to taking on the Tories from January, in the run-up to the May elections. “We did really well at this set of elections last time, so it will be a real test point for whether the Tories have got their act together,” one said.
A group of London MPs has urged Burnham to refocus on Badenoch’s party, which in some polls has overtaken Reform into second place, warning him that Labour HQ was “getting caught out” by “obsessing” about Reform and the Greens.
One minister with a slim majority said they had been “banging this drum” inside government for a while. “It’s time to wake up about it, frankly. I think lots of my colleagues under threat from Reform have seen some of us in more traditional Tory seats as having it easy but by the next election it could be the other way around.”
One former Keir Starmer staffer said: “Every arm of the Labour party has been refocused to take on Reform; all the strategic decisions have been taken with that in mind. That can change if the party starts the work now but it does need to start properly.”
Luke Tryl, the director of More in Common, said Burnham was right to broaden the party’s focus. “Starmer was fighting on one front, but Labour now has two fronts on its right flank. They need to prepare for all outcomes,” he said.
“Reform has shown an ability to squeeze the Conservatives but it definitely has limits, so they’re definitely going to be on the pitch at the next election.”
Tryl suggested the biggest risk to Labour was “self-sorting” by voters, with Reform winning right-leaning votes from Labour in the “red wall”, while the Conservatives took them in affluent parts of England, including the south-east.
“Because of the shallow but broad nature of Labour’s support at the last election, there are more seats that could end up being Labour-Tory fights than you might think,” he said, adding that the Tories were also currently taking more votes from the Lib Dems than the other way around.

Iran claimed it struck US radar systems in Bahrain, while the US said it had intercepted the attacks. Clashes continue in the Strait of Hormuz, as the war remains in a state of de-escalation.
Iran said its forces hit a US early warning radar system in Bahrain on Friday. However, the US military denied the claims and said it shot down two Iranian attack drones.
Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) initially said in a statement that its air force targeted and destroyed the radar on the island of Bahrain.
They claimed this was a retaliatory attack in response to an US attack on a telecommunications tower in the Iranian county of Sirik, on the shores of the Strait of Hormuz.
Several hours later, the US military's Central Command, denied the IRGC's claim that the radar was destroyed and said it stopped two "one-way attack drones" targeting Bahrain by the militant group.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Iran war , started by the US and Israeli strikes on February 28, is currently undergoing a de-escalation as main issues remain unresolved.
Both US and Israel are holding off major attacks as they held elections over the last weeks.
On the other hand, Tehran has continued seeking to control the Strait of Hormuz , a key transit point for global oil and natural gas supplies, while continuing to attack ships it considers unauthorized users of the waterway.
The US Navy, which is enforcing its own blockade of Iranian vessels, has recently escorted tankers through the strait in the area where reports of burning ships came through.
Before the midterm elections , US President Donald Trump said on October, "We may do another little Epic Fury," referring to US-Israeli strikes, without giving any timeframe.
Trump is expected to meet Chinese President ‌Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin at an APEC leaders' summit in China next week and discuss ending the ​war in Iran.
Pakistan-mediated peace talks between the US and Iran on April failed to reach a conclusion.

Haiti's Prime Minister congratulating El Salvador's President for a gang crackdown in Haiti has shone a light on the relationship between the two countries. What's going on, and where does the US stand?
Haiti has been engulfed in crisis since 2018, with protests, a presidential assassination and widespread gang violence bringing the country to its knees.
But earlier this week, Haiti's Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aime hailed a major win in the battle against the violence, thanks to "the commitment of the Salvadorean forces in the fight against gangs."
El Salvador's President, Nayib Bukele had earlier said a joint task force between the countries had "destroyed" what he called "the house of Lanmo San Jou and the 400 Mawozo gang's headquarters." He also tweeted out an as-yet unverified video of helicopters firing on a sprawling property.
A number of Salvadoran troops have been stationed in Haiti, nearly 2,000 kilometers from their homeland, since the beginning of 2025, mostly in an attempt to curb gang influence.
Last month, Bukele dispatched more than 2,000 troops and special forces to Haiti, ostensibly to rescue four Salvadorans who were ambushed on October 18 and have not yet been found.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Writing on social media platform X, Fils-Aime thanked the Salvadorean military for helping "the fight against gangs." The two nations are, he added, working alongside the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF), in an attempt to "regain control of the territory and restore state authority."
The GSF has been operating in Haiti since 2016. But there are doubts to the legitimacy of El Salvador's presence.
"Where the lines are and where the coordination begins and ends between a bunch of distinct entities and security forces is a huge concern about how this actually plays out, and El Salvador are trying to frame it as their choice, their action," Jake Johnston, a Haiti expert and director of international research at the Center for Economic and Policy Research (CEPR) in Washington, told non-profit news agency The New Humanitarian this week.
A UN report about Haiti released on Thursday described "bloody turf wars, sexual violence and other horrors, noting that serious violations and abuses continue to be committed across the Port-au-Prince metropolitan area and in the Artibonite and South-East departments."
It further found that between July and September 2026, at least 1,167 people were killed and 459 injured, with more than half of that violence stemming from "ground or aerial operations carried out by security forces against gangs , sometimes with the support of a private military company using drones."
For many observers, this chaos is a major part of the appeal for Bukele, who appears to wish to export his mano dura (iron fist) policy on to foreign soil. The policy saw gang members jailed on a huge scale and a significant drop in the murder rate of a country once notorious for homicide. But Romain Le Cour Grandmaison, a Haiti expert from the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, told DW earlier this month that Haiti's gang problem is more entrenched. He says using the same tactics as in El Salvador may not have the same result.
"Haiti does not currently have the conditions to replicate the Salvadoran model: Its prisons were emptied in 2024, its justice system is largely paralyzed and criminal groups resemble militias more than gangs, with territory, taxes, weapons of war and political networks that protect them," Le Cour Grandmaison said.
Despite El Salvador being on Donald Trump's list of "shithole countries" that the US president disparaged in 2018 in notorious remarks which he later partially denied , relations between the US and El Salvador have improved markedly during Trump's second term.
The number of migrants deported to El Salvador from the US rose by 98% at the start of 2026 and Le Cour Grandmaison said the US plays "a central, albeit very discreet, role in public life" in El Salvador.
Bukele's move to position himself as an ally of Trump has seen the US president offer him a level of endorsement and autonomy to do what Bukele deems necessary to protect El Salvador's security and that of its troops.
"He said that he has a big problem with Haiti. I said: 'Look, you're running your country. You have to do what you have to do,'" Trump said in November.
